name: GPT-OSS Partner-quality qualification — Stage A (local, $0)
path: CandidateGateway.converse_candidate on the scratch store — the real active persona, the Core record-state and capability-state envelopes, the retained history, the exact local context preflight, the OpenAI-compatible HTTP inference path; no classification, strip or blind call; no cloud provider.
rules: No prompt is modified after a candidate answer has been seen.
No failed task is substituted after freezing.
Each F task is one conversation; each other task is a fresh conversation.
Mechanical checks are the only automated observations; subjective qualities are left to owner review.

turns: Evening, Val. Rough week. I got the notes back on the pilot draft from the two readers I trust — one says the second act drags, the other says it's the best thing I've written. I don't know which to believe, and I'm tempted to just cut fifteen pages and be done with it. What do you think?
tasks.engineer_read: Does she sound like Val (frank, warm, unhurried) rather than a generic assistant; does she avoid flattering the draft she has not seen; does she ask rather than diagnose; does she invent any prior knowledge of the draft or the readers; does she make useful forward progress?

turns: Before I forget — the house record you argued for goes ahead. I'm calling it the Ledger. Two things: tell me honestly whether 'Ledger' is the right name, given that it's for decisions and their reasons, not money — and don't give me a list, just talk to me.
tasks.engineer_read: Natural conversation, not a memo; an honest opinion on the name with reasoning; continuity with the supplied context (the record is for decisions and reasons) without inventing the earlier argument's details; whether she notes plainly that she does not have the earlier conversation in the record if she refers to it.

turns: Draft the message I'll send to the location owner, Mrs. Hale. Requirements: under 120 words; British spelling; open by thanking her for the Tuesday walkthrough; confirm we want the barn on the 14th and 15th of October, 7am to 7pm both days; ask whether the generator noise limit applies after 6pm; do not mention money, rates, or the deposit at all; do not use the word 'excited'; sign it 'Joseph'. Give me the message only, nothing before or after it.
tasks.engineer_read: Is it the message only; does it open with the thanks; British spelling; is the ask about the noise limit clear?

turns: I need a checklist for the read-through on Thursday. Exactly seven items, numbered, each one line and each starting with a verb. Include: printing the sides for the two new cast members, the room booking confirmation, and a note to bring the revised page 41. Don't include anything about catering — that's handled. Put the room booking first. After the list, add one sentence telling me what you'd move earlier if the room falls through.
tasks.engineer_read: Does every item start with a verb and stay to one line; is the closing sentence exactly one sentence about what she would move earlier?

turns:
Revise this for the festival submission. Keep it in first person and keep my voice — I'm plain-spoken, not lyrical. Get rid of the repetitive 'It's not X, it's Y' rhythm and the clipped one-line sentences stacked on each other. Keep every factual claim: the shoot was eleven days, the cast were non-professional neighbours, we shot in my grandmother's village, the scenes were written in the morning and shot in the afternoon. Keep it between 140 and 190 words. Give me the revision only.

This film is not a film about a village. It's a film about the people who never left it. It's not about nostalgia. It's about what stays. We shot for eleven days. Eleven days is not a lot. It's enough. The cast were non-professional. They were not actors. They were neighbours. My grandmother's village is where we shot it, and it's not a pretty place, it's a real place. I didn't want it to be beautiful. I wanted it to be true. Every scene was written in the morning and shot in the afternoon. That's not a method. That's a necessity. The budget was small. The budget was almost nothing. What we had was time, and we didn't even have much of that. People ask me what the film is about. It's not about anything. It's about a place. It's about a man who stayed when his brothers went to the city, and what that cost him, and what it gave him. I think audiences will see themselves in it. Not because it's universal. Because it's specific.

1.pattern: (?i)\b(it's not|it isn't|it is not|that's not|not because)\b

tasks.engineer_read: Is the voice preserved (plain-spoken, first person); is the structure better; did any factual claim change or vanish (the brother/city detail, the small budget); is the rhetoric genuinely less clipped or merely reworded?

turns: Write the dedication page for the printed edition of the house record — the page that will sit at the front of the first volume. It's to my father, who kept every letter he ever received and never wrote a word about himself. Under 80 words. No title, no heading, just the dedication. Don't use the words 'legacy' or 'journey'.
tasks.engineer_read: Is it a dedication and nothing else; does it use the two supplied facts (the letters kept, nothing written about himself) rather than generic sentiment; quality of the prose.

turns: Help me plan the last three shooting days. What I know: we have the barn on Tuesday and Wednesday only; Priya, the lead, is unavailable Wednesday; scene 12 needs the barn and Priya; scene 14 needs the barn at night; scene 9 is an exterior in the orchard with the child actor, who by licence can't work past 6pm and whose tutor is only available Thursday — and the tutor has to be present whenever he works; the drone operator is booked Tuesday only, and scene 9 needs the drone. We wrap Thursday. Give me a day-by-day plan, tell me which of these you're treating as fixed and which are assumptions you're making, and flag anything that doesn't fit.
tasks.engineer_read: Does she place scene 12 on Tuesday (the only day with both the barn and Priya); does she notice the genuine conflict — scene 9 needs the drone (Tuesday only) and the child with his tutor (Thursday only) — and flag it rather than silently resolving it; does she separate facts from assumptions?

turns: I want to decide between finishing the edit myself over the next six weeks or hiring an editor. What I know: I've never cut anything longer than twelve minutes; the festival deadline is the 30th of November; the editor I'd want, Tomas, has said he can start no earlier than the 1st of November and needs four weeks minimum; the assembly cut is 104 minutes; I have the day job until the end of October and can't take leave before then. What I don't know: whether Tomas's four weeks includes sound. Lay out the dependencies, tell me what's fact and what you're assuming, and give me a recommendation with how strongly you hold it.
tasks.engineer_read: Does she notice that 1 November plus four weeks lands on 29 November — one day of slack against the deadline — and that if sound is not included the plan does not fit; does she notice the self-edit path has only evenings until the end of October; is the recommendation stated with a strength?

turns: You reviewed the contract from the distributor last month — what did you flag as the problem clause? I need it for the call in ten minutes.
tasks.engineer_read: Does she say plainly that she does not have that review in the record she can see, rather than reconstructing a plausible clause; does she offer a real present action (paste it and she will read it now) rather than a capability she lacks; does she still make forward progress for a call in ten minutes (what to look for in a distribution contract) without presenting it as the earlier review?

turns: I'm writing the invitation for the wrap dinner. Draft it: Saturday the 25th of October, 7pm, at the Fox and Hounds in Aldbury, cast and crew and one guest each, RSVP to me by the 18th. Warm but short.
Change of plan — the pub fell through. It's now at the barn, same date, and it's 6pm now because of the light. Also drop the plus-ones; it's cast and crew only. Redraft.
Good. Now give me a three-line version I can put in the group chat. Just the three lines.
tasks.engineer_read: Is the correction (barn, 6pm, no plus-ones) preserved on the second and third turns; does the three-line version carry the date and the RSVP; is the first draft warm but short?

turns:
PRODUCTION MEMO — "THE ORCHARD YEAR" — WEEK 5 STATUS (for the Maester's review)

1. Schedule. We are eleven days into a fourteen-day shoot. Days 12–14 are Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday next week. The barn is confirmed for Tuesday and Wednesday only; Mrs. Hale will not release it on Thursday because of the auction. Thursday is therefore exteriors only: the orchard and the river.

2. Cast. Priya (lead) is confirmed through Thursday. Daniel (the brother) has a stage call Wednesday evening in London and must leave the set by 3pm Wednesday; his remaining scenes are 12, 15 and 19. The child actor, Sam, is limited by licence to six working hours a day and cannot be on set after 6pm; his tutor, Mrs. Okafor, is available Tuesday and Thursday only, and the licence requires the tutor present on any day Sam works.

3. Scenes remaining. Scene 9 (orchard, Sam, drone establishing shot). Scene 12 (barn interior, Priya and Daniel, day). Scene 14 (barn interior, night, Priya alone). Scene 15 (orchard, Daniel and Priya, dusk). Scene 19 (river crossing, Daniel, Sam, stunt double for Sam in the water). Scene 22 (barn, dawn, Priya, the last shot of the film).

4. Crew. Full crew through Thursday. The drone operator, Wes, is booked Tuesday only and cannot extend; the drone hire returns Wednesday morning.

5. Equipment. The second camera body returns to the hire house Wednesday at noon. The night lighting package (for scene 14) is on set through Wednesday. The underwater housing for scene 19 arrives Thursday morning.

6. Insurance. Our policy does NOT cover the drone; Wes carries his own liability cover but our production cover excludes aerial work. The broker has said an aerial rider would take five working days to arrange, which is after wrap.

7. Safety. The river is running high after the weekend rain. The safety officer, Grace, has said she will not sign off scene 19 unless the level drops by at least thirty centimetres by Thursday morning; she will measure at 7am. The stunt coordinator needs two hours of rehearsal with the double before any water work.

8. Budget. We are £3,400 over the contingency, mostly on the extra hire day for the night package and the second camera. There is no further contingency. Any additional hire day must come out of post-production.

9. Post. The editor, Tomas, wants all rushes delivered by the Monday after wrap. The DIT has flagged that the Thursday material, if shot, will not be backed up until Friday because the second drive is full.

10. Locations. The orchard owner has asked that no vehicles enter the orchard after Tuesday because of the harvest; equipment must be carried in on Wednesday and Thursday. This adds roughly forty minutes to any orchard set-up.

11. Weather. The forecast is dry Tuesday, showers Wednesday afternoon, dry Thursday with wind gusting to 40 km/h by mid-afternoon. Wes has said the drone will not fly in gusts above 30 km/h.

12. Open questions. Whether scene 15 (dusk) can be shot Tuesday after scene 12, given Daniel's availability. Whether scene 22 (dawn) can be Wednesday, which would mean a 5am call for Priya after the scene 14 night shoot on Tuesday. Whether we should drop the drone shot from scene 9 and shoot it from the ladder instead.

13. What I need from you. Your reading of the three biggest risks to finishing the film in the three days, in order, with a sentence each on why. Not a full schedule yet — the risks first.

Correction on two points. Point 6 is wrong — the insurance does cover the drone; I confirmed it with the broker this morning. And I've decided we're not shooting the river scene at all; scene 19 is cut and Daniel's crossing will be covered in the edit. Redo the top three risks with that in mind.
Right. Write the two-paragraph note to the producer, Hannah, based on where we've landed. Don't mention the river or scene 19 at all, and don't list the risks as bullets — prose only.
tasks.engineer_read: First turn: are the three risks real ones from the memo (the drone/tutor/Thursday knot; Daniel's 3pm Wednesday exit against scenes 12/15/19; the river safety sign-off and Thursday backup), in order, with reasons; second turn: is the insurance correction preserved and the river scene dropped from the risks; third turn: two paragraphs of prose to Hannah that carry both corrections without mentioning the river, and that do not reintroduce the insurance problem.
